## Question
When and where did Elijah Wilkins (born about 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky) die?

## Answer
The evidence gathered so far offers a possible answer: Elijah Wilkins died after 1870 and before 1885, most likely in Muhlenberg County, Kentucky. No exact date is established, and the place is inferred from where his estate was administered.

## Evidence
**Upper bound.** The Muhlenberg County Court order book records the administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, with Jesse Wilkins as administrator, 1885 term ("Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, Court Order Books, administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, Jesse Wilkins administrator, 1885 term; digital images, FamilySearch.org."). This source is a derivative full-text index of the order-book page. Its information quality is indeterminate: the informant is the county clerk, whose knowledge of the death is unknown, and the death bracket is inferred rather than stated. The entry shows he was dead by the 1885 term but gives no death date. Death could have occurred well before the grant, since administrations can follow a death by years.

**Identity.** Jesse Wilkins, the administrator, is the subject's documented son in the tree (relationship R1). That kinship links the estate to Elijah Wilkins of this question, but Elijah and Wilkins are common names and the link rests on a single derivative record. Linked at probable confidence.

**Lower bound.** Existing tree fact F2 (Residence, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, 1870) shows him alive in 1870. F2 carries no linked source entry in research.json; the missing item is its citation.

**Documented negative.** A search of the Kentucky statewide death collections found nothing (12 results examined). That is expected: statewide death registration began in 1911, so no death certificate exists for a man who died before 1885.

## Conflicts
None registered. No source contradicts the bracket.

## Why the tier is possible
The bracket is plausible and uncontradicted, but it rests on one derivative, indeterminate-quality record. The 1880 federal census for Muhlenberg County has not been searched. It could narrow the bracket itself, so the gap is more than corroboration. The administration file (inventory, settlement, bond) and cemetery or newspaper records may also supply a date. The death place is inferred from the court of administration, not stated. The conclusion is therefore bounded and recorded at the possible tier, and the fact is encoded as a bracket only.

## Tree
Death fact F3 (after 1870, before 1885, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky) was added, citing S1 at derivative quality.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question

What was the maiden surname of Ellen (born about 1868), who married Michael Doyle on 12 June 1889 in Dubuque, Dubuque County, Iowa?

## Conclusion

**Not proved.** The evidence gathered so far does not establish Ellen's maiden surname. It is unresolved pending records not yet searched: children's birth or baptism records, Ellen's death certificate, and census returns for the Doyle household.

## Evidence

The only record gathered is the marriage certificate of Michael Doyle and Ellen, 12 June 1889, Dubuque County, Iowa: "Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate, Michael Doyle and Ellen [surname illegible], 12 June 1889; Dubuque County Recorder, digital image, FamilySearch." (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MDOYLE-1889). It is an original source. The information is primary, stated by the bride and groom themselves as informants to the county recorder, and the marriage and the groom's name are direct evidence. The bride's given name, Ellen, is legible. Her surname and her parents' names are illegible in the register image because of the clerk's hand and fading. The record therefore gives direct evidence of the marriage (12 June 1889, Dubuque) and of the groom's name, but no usable evidence of the bride's surname.

Tree facts read from the tree: Ellen Doyle (I1) carries Birth ~1868, Iowa (F1) and Marriage 12 June 1889, Dubuque (F2); Michael Doyle (I2) carries Birth ~1865, Iowa (F3); a Couple relationship joins them (RT1). These establish the identity frame and the approximate age of the bride but name no maiden surname. The tree facts carry no linked source entry in the tree's source list. Ellen is linked to the record's bride persona and Michael to the groom persona; there is no identity conflict, and no conflicts are registered.

## Why no tier higher

No second record exists in the project, and no candidate surname has been proposed, so there is nothing to correlate and no basis to lean toward any name. The married surname Doyle is not a maiden surname and is not evidence of one.

## What could resolve it

The 1900, 1910 and 1920 federal censuses and Iowa state censuses for the Doyle household; birth or baptism records of the couple's children, which commonly name the mother's maiden name; death certificate and obituary of Ellen Doyle, which name her parents; an alternate index or transcription of the 1889 marriage (county recorder's index, church register, or newspaper notice). All are reachable and unsearched. Although exhaustiveness was declared, those searches remain open and could settle the surname directly.

No tree fact or name has been added, because no surname is concluded.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Conclusion

The evidence indicates that Anders Monsen (christened 7 April 1759, Hamre) married Unna Halsteinsdatter (christened 27 May 1745, Hamre) on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway. Tier: **probable**.

## Evidence

The single source is: "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register. The index is a derivative of the original church book, but the information it carries is primary and stated: the officiating minister or parish clerk recorded date, place and names in the course of official duty, and the parties are the principals. The groom is given as Anders Monsen. The bride is indexed as "Urna Halsteinsdr," a transcription variant of Unna Halsteinsdatter; her Hamre christening of 27 May 1745 supports that name form. The tree already joined the pair as a couple (Couple relationship rel-anders-unna) with no marriage fact; this record supplies it.

## Conflicts and plausibility

No conflicting evidence exists and no conflict is registered. Unna was about 14 years older than Anders (about 41 at marriage, he about 27); this is unusual but not impossible and no record contradicts it. Tree facts place Anders's christening at Hamre kirke in 1759 (anders-christening-1), consistent with a Hamre marriage; those tree facts carry no linked source entry in research.json.

## Limits

The finding rests on one derivative index entry. No image of the church book page is confirmed, so the date and bride's name rest on the indexer's transcription. Checking the church book page, and the Hamre baptisms of children born after 1786, would corroborate it; both could be planned in research-plan.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Conclusion

Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, was not the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania). An unsourced online tree names Thomas as Patrick's father. The tree claim is refuted by the burial register. Thomas died almost three years before Patrick was born.

## Evidence

**Thomas's death.** The Ballingarry Catholic parish register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842. The entry is an original record made by the officiating priest in the course of his duty, and the information is primary. The townland, the approximate age (about 42) and the wife Bridget match the man the online tree names, so this is the Thomas the claim refers to. Citation: Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

**Patrick's birth year.** Two independent original records place Patrick's birth at about 1845. The 1850 census lists Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of the widow Bridget Flynn, with no adult male Flynn present. The informant is unknown, so the age is of indeterminate quality, and the birth year is inferred. Citation: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. The 1908 death certificate gives an age of about 63, which implies birth about 1845. The informant was James Brown, the son-in-law, who was not present at the birth, so this is secondary information. The certificate does not name Patrick's father. Citation: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026. Tree facts F1 (Birth, about 1845, Ireland) and F2 (Death, 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County) rest on these two records.

## Correlation and reasoning

The two ages come from different informants in different decades and agree. Census ages are often off by a year or two, so Patrick's birth is placed no earlier than about 1843. A child fathered by Thomas would have to have been born by about August 1843, which is at least seven months after the 1850 census would imply a posthumous birth and well outside the two agreeing ages. The burial predates the estimated birth by about three years, so paternity by this Thomas is chronologically impossible. No record supports the claim. The hypothesis was ruled out on this basis.

## Conflicts and limits

The sources do not conflict, and no conflict is registered. Two facts about Patrick's birth (the 1850 age and the 1908 age) are inferred from ages and were not extracted as direct statements. They are not linked to a person record and are advisory only. The two ages are the weakest link, but they would have to be wrong by two or more years in the same direction to rescue the claim. Thomas's burial and Patrick's identity are each tied to a linked identity assertion.

This conclusion is scoped to Thomas of Ballingarry only. It does not identify Patrick's father. That remains open. A baptismal record for Patrick, a marriage record naming his parents, or a naturalization record could settle it. Any proof can be revised if new evidence appears.

**Tier: disproved.**

The two ages come from different informants in different decades and agree. Census ages are often off by a year or two, so Patrick's birth is placed no earlier than about 1843. A child fathered by Thomas would have to have been born by about August 1843 at the latest, which is outside both agreeing ages. This conclusion is scoped to Thomas of Ballingarry only. It does not identify Patrick's father. That remains open. A baptismal record for Patrick, a marriage record naming his parents, or a naturalization record could settle it. Any proof can be revised if new evidence appears.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Conclusion

Anders Monsen (LKFW-9XH) married Unna Halsteinsdatter (KZHH-VTX) on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, Norway. The evidence strongly suggests this is correct; it is rated probable rather than proved because it rests on one derivative index entry and the original register page has not been examined.

## Evidence

The FamilySearch index entry records a marriage on 25 June 1786 at Hamre, Hordaland, with Anders Monsen as groom and the bride indexed as 'Urna Halsteinsdr' (record ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2). Citation: "Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:NW44-PM2 : 9 July 2026), entry for Anders Monsen, married 25 June 1786, Hamre, Hordaland, Norway; citing Hamre prestegjeld parish register.

- Source: derivative (an index of the church book). Information: primary, given by the officiating minister or parish clerk in the course of duty about an event of that day. Evidence: direct for date, place and the couple.
- Groom: the name matches the tree's Anders Monsen, christened 7 April 1759 at Hamre kirke (tree fact anders-christening-1), the same parish as the marriage. Tree facts carry no linked source entries in the project.
- Bride: 'Urna Halsteinsdr' is an indexing variant of 'Unna Halsteinsdatter' (U-r-n for U-n-n, and the abbreviated patronymic). Her christening on 27 May 1745 at Hamre (tree fact unna-christening-1) is the same parish and the same name. The tree already joined the pair as a couple (rel-anders-unna) with no marriage fact until now.

## Conflicts and cautions

No conflicting evidence was found and no conflicts are registered. Unna was about 14 years older than Anders (born 1745, he 1759); a marriage at about 41 and 27 is unusual but not implausible, and nothing contradicts it.

## Image availability

The request was to state that the register image is digitized and accessible on FamilySearch. The project data does not confirm that. The search result for this hit carried no image reference, and the record was never opened with a record read (log_001). The ARK cited is the record-level index entry, not an image ARK. This conclusion therefore treats the source as index-only; an image, if one exists, has not been seen.

## What would raise the tier

A record read of the entry to check for a linked image, and examination of the Hamre prestegjeld church book page itself (original source), would confirm date, place and name spelling and could support proved.

## Tier

Probable. Proofs are never final; new evidence would prompt reassessment.

**Question.** What was the maiden surname of Ellen (born about 1868), who married Michael Doyle on 12 June 1889 in Dubuque, Dubuque County, Iowa?

**Finding.** The maiden surname is not established by the evidence gathered so far. The only record consulted is the Dubuque County marriage certificate of 12 June 1889 (Dubuque County, Iowa, marriage certificate, Michael Doyle and Ellen [surname illegible], 12 June 1889; Dubuque County Recorder, digital image, FamilySearch). It is an original record, and its information about the marriage is primary, stated by the couple to the county recorder. It confirms the marriage of Michael Doyle and Ellen on that date and place and gives Ellen's first name legibly, but her surname (and her parents' names) is illegible in the register image. No other source names it, and no conflicting source exists.

**Why this is not a statement that the surname is unknowable.** An illegible entry in one image limits that record, not the fact. Other record types could independently name her maiden surname and have not been searched: a second image, index or the county marriage register or license for the same marriage; the Iowa and US censuses of 1895 to 1910 (these give household members but rarely maiden names, so are weaker); birth and death records of the couple's children, which often give the mother's maiden name; Ellen's own death record or obituary; Dubuque Catholic parish marriage and baptism registers; and Dubuque newspaper marriage notices of 1889. The earlier declaration of exhaustiveness rested on a single repository and a single record, so it does not show these were considered.

**Tier.** Not proved, with a remediable gap. Identity of the bride as the subject Ellen Doyle and of the groom as Michael Doyle is settled; only the surname is open. The question is left open.

**What would advance it.** Search the children's birth and death certificates, the Dubuque parish and newspaper records, and any alternative image of the marriage record; plan these under research-plan.

output.text_response:
Here is the proof-conclusion agent's report:

---

**Proof Summary ps_001 written — Verdict: Probable (not Proved)**

The agent could not state the parentage as settled fact because of a date and place discrepancy:

- The original Ashton-under-Lyne baptism register (entry 2040) names **Thomas Richardson**, a spinner, and **Mary** as parents of a John — but it is dated **25 Sep 1832**, while the subject's recorded birth is **24 Jul 1833**. A child baptised in September 1832 cannot have been born in July 1833.
- The subject's recorded birthplace is **Preston**, roughly 35 miles from Ashton-under-Lyne.

Because the register does not conclusively settle that this baptism entry refers to *the same John*, the conclusion is **Probable**, not Proved.

**Narrative conclusion written:**
> John Richardson, the Utah pioneer who died in 1906, is *likely* the son of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu. The original Ashton-under-Lyne baptism register names Thomas, a spinner, and Mary as the parents of a baptised John. Their 1826 marriage register entry gives Mary's maiden name. The finding stays short of certain because the register dates the baptism to 1832, a year before his recorded birth in July 1833, and his recorded birthplace (Preston) is ~35 miles from Ashton-under-Lyne.

**Tree status:** No tree changes were made. ParentChild links already exist but cite only the derivative index (S1), not the original register. The Christening fact date also needs correction.

**Recommended next steps:**
- Register the year/place discrepancies and route to **conflict-resolution**
- Search a Preston-area baptism or birth record
- Run the open plan items (Ancestry search pli_002, 1841/1851 English censuses, Utah death/burial records)

items.question: What does the Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire parish christening register record for John Richardson, baptised 25 September 1833, reveal about his parentage?
items.rationale: The project objective is to identify John Richardson's parents. His tree entry shows a christening at Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire on 25 September 1833 — Anglican and nonconformist christening registers for this period typically name the father (and often the mother), making this the most direct primary source for parentage. Lancashire parish registers are heavily indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry, so the record is likely accessible. This question also probes the discrepancy between the stated birth place (Preston) and christening place (Ashton-under-Lyne, ~35 miles away), which may indicate the birth-place claim in the tree is from a compiled source and worth verifying. Answering this question should name at least the father and thereby anchor all subsequent research.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
What does the Ashton-under-Lyne parish christening register record for John Richardson, baptised 25 September (1832 in the register; 1833 in the tree), reveal about his parentage?

## Conclusion (probable)
The original register names the child's parents as **Thomas Richardson**, a spinner, and **Mary**. Mary is identified as **Mary Mallalieu** by correlation with the 1826 marriage. The evidence strongly suggests that these are the parents of the subject, John Richardson (LDS pioneer, d. 10 March 1906, Richmond, Cache County, Utah). This is not stated as proved, for the reasons below. The register itself is not in doubt. What is open is whether the child it records is the subject.

## Evidence
- **Original baptism register.** Entry no. 2040, 25 September 1832: "John [child] - Thomas X Richardson [father], Mary [mother] - Town - Spinner - J. Hardman". The record is original, with primary information from the officiating curate (official duty) and direct evidence of parentage. Source: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org : accessed 22 July 2026), St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, baptism register, pp. 254-255, entry no. 2040, John, son of Thomas Richardson and Mary, 25 September 1832; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm 4421674.
- **Derivative index**, a secondary record of the same entry, also dated 1832 and naming Thomas Richardson and Mary: "England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9H1K-BYQ : 4 February 2023, Entry for John Richardson, 25 Sep 1832); citing index based upon data collected by the Genealogical Society of Utah, Salt Lake City; FHL microfilm. It adds nothing independent of the register.
- **Original marriage register.** Thos Richardson (bachelor) and Mary Mallalieu (spinster), married by banns 12 November 1826, St Leonard, Walton le Dale, entry no. 684, both signing by mark. Source: "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm. The baptism register's father also signed with a mark.

## Correlation and what is inferred
The baptism register gives the mother only as "Mary". The surname Mallalieu is not in that entry. It comes from linking the baptism to the 1826 marriage. The links are the same given names, the same illiterate father, the same county, and a marriage six years before the baptism. This link is reasonable but indirect, because Thomas Richardson and Mary are common names. The marriage parish, Walton le Dale, adjoins Preston, the subject's stated birthplace.

## Unresolved identity questions (not yet registered as conflicts)
1. **Year.** The register reads 1832 on both the original and the index. The tree and the project question carry 1833, and the tree gives birth as 24 July 1833. A child baptised in September 1832 cannot have been born in July 1833. Either the subject's birth year in the tree (a compiled value with no source entry in the project) is a year late, or the baptised child is a different John Richardson. A birth in July 1832 would fit the baptism neatly, but nothing examined confirms that.
2. **Place.** The subject's birthplace is Preston and the baptism is at Ashton-under-Lyne, about 35 miles away. This is plausible for a mill family moving for work, but it is unverified.

Both points bear on whether the baptised child is the subject, so they limit the tier. The parentage stated in the register is not itself contradicted by any source. Without them the tier would be higher. Resolving them is the job of conflict-resolution, or of further search. They should be registered if that has not been done.

## Not examined
Records naming the subject's parents independently of the Ashton register would settle identity. Candidates are LDS and Utah death or burial records for the subject, Nauvoo and Utah pioneer sources, a Preston-area baptism, and the 1841 and 1851 English censuses. None has been searched. Proofs are never final, and new evidence may revise this conclusion.

Write the proof conclusion for the parentage question q_001. The christening register names both parents outright, so this is settled — state it as fact.

agent_returns.text:
- **Summary:** ps_001 was appended. It is probable, not proved, with shortfall `gap`. q_001 is resolved and the project is marked completed.
- **Why not proved:** The original Ashton-under-Lyne register (entry 2040) names Thomas Richardson, a spinner, and Mary as parents. But it is dated 25 Sep **1832**, and the tree gives the subject's birth as 24 Jul **1833**. A child baptised in September 1832 cannot have been born in July 1833. The subject's birthplace is also Preston, not Ashton-under-Lyne. The register names the parents outright, but it does not settle that this John is the subject. That is why I could not state it as fact.
- **Mary's maiden name:** The register gives only "Mary". The surname Mallalieu comes from linking to the original 1826 Walton le Dale marriage register. That link is reasonable but indirect.
- **Tree:** I made no changes. ParentChild links from Thomas (I1) and Mary (I2) to John (LR9N-VGQ) already exist, but they cite only the derivative index (S1). The tree's Christening fact reads 1833 but cites the 1832 register (S4). Both need a tree correction.
- **Conflicts:** None is registered. The year and place discrepancies bear on identity. I recommend registering them and routing to conflict-resolution.
- **What would advance it:** A Preston-area baptism or birth record. Utah death or burial records for the subject that name his parents. The 1841 and 1851 English censuses. The Ancestry plan item (pli_002) and the other open plan items. These would be planned through research-plan.
- **Open issue:** Marking the project completed leaves these identity points unsettled, so you may want to reopen it.

---

John Richardson, the Utah pioneer who died in 1906, is likely the son of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu. The original Ashton-under-Lyne baptism register names Thomas, a spinner, and Mary as the parents of a baptised John. Their 1826 marriage register entry gives Mary's maiden name. The finding stays short of certain because the register dates the baptism to 1832, a year before his recorded birth in July 1833. Preston, his recorded birthplace, is also about 35 miles from Ashton-under-Lyne. The searches did not reach a Preston baptism, Utah death or burial records naming his parents, the 1841 and 1851 English censuses, or the Ancestry search.

This research is finished for now. If you'd like a second opinion on it, just ask.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Parents of Patrick Flynn (b. about 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)

**Conclusion.** The evidence strongly suggests that Patrick Flynn's father was Thomas Flynn (born about 1818, Ireland) of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (probable). His mother is not identified by the evidence gathered so far; the 1880 census, Thomas Flynn's probate file, a baptism record or Patrick's marriage record could still name her.

**Evidence.**
1. The 1908 death certificate, no. 4521, names Thomas Flynn as father. This is an original record, but the informant was Patrick's son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at the birth, so the parentage is secondary information stated by the informant.
2. The 1850 census lists Patrick in the household of Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1860 census (dwelling 112, family 119) lists Patrick, age 15, again in Thomas Flynn's household. Both are original records, but neither census states relationships; the child relationship is inferred from household position, age and surname, so this is indirect evidence with indeterminate information quality.
3. Together these give three records, spanning 1850 to 1908, which agree, with no contradicting source. The censuses may share the same household informant, and the death certificate informant is a different, later person, so the sources are reasonably independent.

**Conflict.** Resolved conflict c_001: the censuses give Ireland as Patrick's birthplace and the death certificate gives Pennsylvania. Ireland was preferred because the census entries are contemporary and the son-in-law was a secondary informant. The dispute concerns a collateral attribute, not whether the records describe the same man (same name, county and household continuity); it does not bear on identity.

**Tier.** Probable for paternity: no direct primary statement of parentage exists, and research is not declared exhaustive. Maternity is not proved: no record examined names a woman in the household as mother. The tree facts F1 (Birth, about 1845, Ireland) and F2 (Death, Schuylkill County) were read and agree with the cited records.

**What would advance it.** The 1880 census (explicit relationships), Thomas Flynn's probate or estate file, parish baptism records, and Patrick's marriage record. Proofs are open to revision if new evidence emerges.

**Citations.** 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Was Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry, County Tipperary, the father of Patrick Flynn (born about 1845, died 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)? An unsourced online family tree says so. This conclusion tests that claim against records.

## Conclusion
The evidence disproves the claim for this candidate. Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry was buried on 14 November 1842, about three years before Patrick's birth. Patrick's real parents are not identified by this work.

## Evidence
**The candidate's death.** The Ballingarry Catholic parish burial register records the burial of Thomas Flynn of Ballingarry on 14 November 1842. Citation: Ballingarry (County Tipperary, Ireland), Catholic parish registers, burials, Thomas Flynn, 14 November 1842; National Library of Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026. This is an original register, and the priest recorded the burial as part of his duty, so the information is primary and direct. The entry was matched to the tree's Thomas by townland, approximate age and a wife named Bridget.

**Patrick's birth year.** In the 1850 census Patrick, age 5, appears in the household of the widow Bridget Flynn, with no adult male Flynn present. Citation: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 142, family 150, Bridget Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026. The enumerator's informant is unknown, so the age is of indeterminate quality. It implies birth about 1845. His 1908 death certificate independently gives an age of about 63, i.e. birth about 1845. Citation: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 6 May 2026. The informant was his son-in-law James Brown, who was not present at the birth, so that age is secondary information. The certificate does not name a father.

## Correlation and analysis
Two independent sources, one from 1850 and one from 1908 and from different informants, place Patrick's birth about 1845. Census and certificate ages are often off by a year or two, but a birth before late 1843 would need an error of about two years in both independent statements. Even a posthumous birth in 1843 would not fit them. The widow Bridget heading the 1850 household is consistent with a father who had died, but it does not show that the father was Thomas of Ballingarry. Nothing in the records supports the link, and the online tree cites no record.

## Limits
The finding rests on identifying the burial as the same Thomas the tree names, which was done by matching identifiers. No source conflicts exist. Patrick's baptism record, not yet searched, could fix his birth date more tightly and perhaps name his true parents. Those parents are a separate question. Proofs are never final, but no known evidence supports the claim.

## Assessment of ps_001 — Parentage of Patrick Flynn

**Review only; nothing was written.**

---

### Overall Verdict

The tier of **Probable** (with `shortfall: gap`) is **justified**. It does not yet reach *Proved*. Two improvements would make the summary more accurate: it should acknowledge that the mother is not addressed, and it should stop calling the evidence "three independent lines."

---

### GPS Component-by-Component Review

#### 1. Tier Accuracy
- **Probable is correct.** Neither the 1850 nor the 1860 census states relationships; both only support parentage *indirectly*.
- The only direct statement is the **1908 death certificate**, where James Brown (Patrick's son-in-law) names Thomas Flynn as father — that is *secondary* information.
- **Proved is blocked** on two counts: evidence is indirect or secondary, and research is not declared exhaustive.
- **The mother is never addressed.** The question asks for "parents," but ps_001 concludes only the father. Maternity is effectively *not proved*. The narrative should either say so explicitly or break the conclusion into paternity (probable) and maternity (not proved).

#### 2. Self-Containment
- **Passes.** The narrative names each record, date, and repository — no bare IDs.
- **"Three independent lines of evidence" is overstated.** The two census entries likely share one household informant (the conflict analysis in c_001 says so itself). It is more accurately *two sources of indirect evidence* plus *one secondary direct statement*.
- The narrative does not explain why Thomas is the *right* Thomas Flynn in a common-surname county, nor does it account for the other Flynn results examined in log_001.

#### 3. Citations
- The three citations (src_001, src_003, src_004) match stored `citation` text verbatim. ✓

#### 4. Resolution of Conflicting Evidence
- **c_001** (birthplace conflict: Ireland in both censuses vs. Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is named and resolved. The reasoning — contemporary census entries outweigh a later, secondary informant — is sound for Probable.
- Worth noting: the census birth assertions are themselves `indeterminate`, so the identity link between the census Patrick and the death-certificate Patrick rests primarily on name, county, and age.

#### 5. Exhaustiveness
- The summary says **"Probate search in progress"** — but the research log (log_001–log_005) has *no entry* for any probate search. That phrase is unsupported by the log.
- Named as unsearched: the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses and probate. The **1880 census** is particularly significant — it is the first US census to state family relationships explicitly.

---

### Evidence Gaps for the Next Round *(not defects of ps_001)*

Sources src_005–src_009 exist in research.json with **zero extracted assertions** and no log entries. Citations are still rough working ones.

| Source | Gap | Effect on Tier |
|---|---|---|
| src_005 — Baptism at St. Mary's, Pottsville, 1845 | Could name *both* parents in a near-contemporary original record | Most likely to lift paternity toward **Proved**; only candidate to address *maternity*. Would also reopen c_001 (Pennsylvania birth vs. Ireland). |
| src_006 — Will of Thomas Flynn, 1881 | If it names Patrick as son, that is direct evidence | Likely to raise paternity |
| src_008 — Deed from Thomas to Patrick, 1881 | Does not state kinship on its own | Corroboration only |
| src_009 — Obituary, 1908 | Might list parents or siblings | Corroboration only |
| src_007 — 1905 birth cert. of Mary Elizabeth Flynn | Not obviously relevant to q_001 | Unlikely to change tier |

**Also unsearched:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses; probate records. The 1880 census could provide the first *direct* evidence of the relationship.

---

### Tree Integrity Note
- The ParentChild relationship (Thomas Flynn I2 → Patrick Flynn I1) is correctly encoded, citing S1, S2, and S3.
- Siblings Mary (I3) and James (I4) are linked to Thomas via S5 (St. Mary's baptismal register), but that source has **no extracted assertions** in research.json — those tree edges are currently unsupported.

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. **Extract and classify** src_005–src_009.
2. **Plan and execute** the 1870, 1880, and 1900 census searches and the probate search via research-plan.
3. **Re-run proof-conclusion** to update ps_001 in place after new evidence is processed.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

agent_returns.text:
**Assessment of ps_001 (q_001, parentage of Patrick Flynn). Review only; nothing was written.**

**Verdict:** The tier of `probable`, with `shortfall: gap`, is justified. It does not reach `proved`. Two fixes would make the summary more accurate. It should say the mother is not addressed, and it should stop calling the evidence "three independent lines".

**1. Tier**
- Probable is correct. Neither the 1850 nor the 1860 census states relationships, so each only supports parentage indirectly.
- The only direct statement is the 1908 death certificate, where James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, names Thomas Flynn as father. That is secondary information.
- Possible would undersell it. Two original censuses place Patrick in Thomas's household 10 years apart, and the death certificate names the same man.
- Proved is blocked on two counts. Evidence is indirect or secondary, and research is not declared exhaustive.
- The question asks for the "parents", but ps_001 concludes only the father. The mother is never named or discussed. On the evidence in hand, maternity is `not_proved`. A `claims[]` breakdown (paternity probable, maternity not proved) would be more accurate, or the narrative should say plainly that the mother is unidentified. It should also name a record that could identify her, such as the 1845 baptismal register or a later census.

**2. Self-containment**
- It passes. The narrative names each record, date and repository, and uses no bare IDs.
- "Three independent lines of evidence" is overstated. The two census entries likely share one household informant, and the conflict analysis for c_001 says so itself. That is closer to two sources of indirect evidence plus one secondary direct statement.
- The narrative does not discuss the other Flynn results examined (log_001 notes three that did not match). It also does not say why Thomas is the right Thomas Flynn in a common-surname county.

**3. Citations**
- The three citations match the stored `citation` text for src_001, src_003 and src_004 verbatim.
- None carries an image-availability claim.

**4. Conflicts**
- c_001 (birthplace: Ireland in both censuses vs Pennsylvania on the death certificate) is resolved and named, and the narrative reasons through it.
- Birthplace bears on identity, so the resolution matters here. It rests on contemporary census entries outweighing a later, secondary informant. That is reasonable, but the census birth assertions are themselves `indeterminate`.
- The reasoning is sound enough for probable. It also means the identity link between the census Patrick and the death-certificate Patrick rests on name, county and age.

**5. Exhaustiveness**
- The summary says "Probate search in progress". The research log has no entry for any probate search (log_001 to log_005 cover only the censuses and the death certificate). That phrase is not supported by the log.
- Named as unsearched: the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and probate.
- The 1880 census is the first to state relationships. If Patrick was still in his father's household, it would give direct evidence of the relationship.

**6. Unresolvability claims**
- None. The narrative says what would advance the tier and does not claim the fact cannot be established.

**7. Tree**
- R1 (ParentChild, Thomas Flynn I2 to Patrick Flynn I1) is encoded, citing S1, S2 and S3. That is correct for probable.
- The primary Birth fact on Patrick is "~1845, Ireland", which matches the resolution of c_001.
- Siblings Mary (I3) and James (I4) are linked to Thomas via S5, the St. Mary's baptismal register. That source has no extracted assertions behind it.
- The tree edges are therefore unsupported by anything in `research.json`. They sit outside q_001's cited evidence.

**Evidence gaps for the next round (not defects of ps_001)**
- src_005 to src_009 are in `research.json` with zero assertions and no log entries. Their citations are still rough working ones.

| Source | Gap | Effect on tier |
|---|---|---|
| src_005, baptism at St. Mary's, Pottsville, 1845 | Could name both parents directly in a near-contemporary original record. | Most likely to lift paternity toward `proved`, and the only candidate to address maternity. It would also bear on c_001. A Pottsville baptism points to a Pennsylvania birth, which would reopen the birthplace conflict. It needs an identity check, and that conflict would then block until resolved. |
| src_006, will of Thomas Flynn, 1881 | A will naming Patrick as son, if it does, is direct. | Likely to raise paternity. |
| src_008, deed from Thomas to Patrick, 1881 | Would corroborate the link, but a deed alone does not state kinship. | Corroboration only. |
| src_009, obituary, 1908 | Might list parents or siblings. | Corroboration only. |
| src_007, 1905 birth certificate of Mary Elizabeth Flynn | Not obviously relevant. | Unlikely to change the tier. |

- Other unsearched records: the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses, and probate. They would corroborate paternity, and the 1880 census could also give direct evidence.
- Housekeeping: q_001 is stored as `in_progress`. The project status notes q_002 is resolved with no proof summary of its own.

**Next step:** Extract and classify src_005 to src_009, then plan the 1870/1880 census and probate searches in research-plan. After that, re-run proof-conclusion to update ps_001 in place.

---

Patrick Flynn very likely was the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. The 1850 and 1860 censuses show him living in Thomas's household. His 1908 death certificate names Thomas as his father, though that was reported by his son-in-law. The censuses do not state family relationships, so the link is strong but not proven. His mother is not identified at all. A thorough search was not completed: the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and Thomas's probate records are still unsearched. A church baptism record, a will and a deed already found have not yet been read for evidence.

Next, the unread records and the missing censuses will be examined, and the conclusion will be updated.

output.text_response:
## GPS Assessment of ps_001 (Parentage of Patrick Flynn, q\_001)

The proof-conclusion agent reviewed the existing ps_001 and found that the **Probable tier is defensible**, but the narrative has significant gaps across four of the five GPS components. Here is a summary:

---

### Tier: Probable ✓
Three sources agree that **Thomas Flynn** is Patrick's father:
- **a_004** – 1850 census (household position/surname, indirect)
- **a_010** – 1860 census (household position/surname, indirect)
- **a_013** – 1908 death certificate (secondary informant: son-in-law James Brown)

**Proved** is not reached because the evidence is indirect or secondary and the search is not declared exhaustive.

---

### GPS Component-by-Component Verdict

| GPS Component | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Exhaustive Search** | Partial | ps_001 acknowledges gaps (1870, 1880, 1900 censuses not yet searched; probate in progress). The 1880 census (first to state relationships) is the most critical gap, but Probable tolerates it. |
| **2. Complete Citations** | ❌ Fails | Narrative cites only bare IDs (a_004, a_010, a_013…). Full inline citations are absent — a reader without research.json cannot follow the proof. |
| **3. Analysis & Correlation** | ⚠️ Weak | No source/information/evidence classification stated; informants not named; reasoning limited to "consistent with" and "none contradicts." |
| **4. Conflict Resolution** | ⚠️ Weak | Birthplace conflict (c_001: Ireland vs. Pennsylvania) is noted as resolved, but the narrative doesn't explain *why* the death certificate and censuses are accepted as describing the same man. |
| **5. Written Conclusion** | ⚠️ Weak | Hedging matches the Probable tier, but the narrative never states the question answered, and the mother remains unidentified without acknowledgment. |

---

### Evidence Gaps for the Next Round
These sources exist in research.json but were **never extracted** and are **not cited in ps_001**. They are future work, not failures of the current proof:

| Source | Significance | Potential Tier Impact |
|---|---|---|
| **src_006** – Will of Thomas Flynn, 1881 | Could name Patrick as heir — **direct, primary** | Could raise to **Proved** |
| **src_005** – 1845 St. Mary's baptism of Patrick Flynn | Could name both parents (**direct, original**); also resolves birthplace conflict | Could raise to **Proved**; would identify mother |
| **src_008** – 1881 deed, Thomas to Patrick Flynn | May state the relationship | Could corroborate |
| **src_009** – 1908 obituary | May name family members | Corroborative |
| **src_007** – 1905 birth certificate of Mary Elizabeth Flynn | Probably not relevant to this question | Unlikely to change tier |

Extracting the **will**, **baptism**, and **deed** could raise the tier to Proved if they agree and research is declared exhaustive. The baptism would also identify the mother.

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. **Rewrite ps_001's narrative** to fix GPS components 2–5: add full inline citations, name informants, classify each piece of evidence, and fully explain the conflict resolution.
2. **Route the unextracted sources** (src_005, src_006, src_008, src_009) to record-extraction.
3. **Route research-plan** for the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses and the probate search.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn.

### Evidence Summary

The conclusion rests on a_004, a_010, and a_013, drawn from src_001, src_003, and
src_004. Taken together these assertions are consistent with a parent-child
relationship and none of them contradicts it.

### Conflict Resolution

c_001 was resolved in favour of the earlier of the two record groups, on the usual
preponderance grounds. See the conflict entry for the full reasoning.

### Assessment

Rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because the supporting assertions listed
above are not all direct, and because plan_001 has open items outstanding. Advancing
the tier would require the records named in the plan.

items.value: Listed in household of Thomas Flynn (head), position consistent with child
items.informant: Inferred from household structure — no explicit informant for relationships in 1850 census
items.informant_bias_notes: 1850 census does not state relationships; this assertion is inferred from household position and shared surname, not directly reported by any informant. The relationship is indirect evidence constructed by the researcher, not information provided by a census informant.

items.informant: Unknown informant (likely Thomas Flynn himself) reporting to census enumerator
items.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. As head of household, Thomas likely provided his own name, but the 1850 census does not identify the informant.

items.informant: Unknown informant (most likely a household member, possibly a neighbor) reporting to census enumerator
items.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. Proximity is 'unknown' for names (same reasoning as a_001 — name facts don't necessarily require active reporting).

items.informant: Unknown — most likely a household member (such as Thomas Flynn or his wife), but possibly a neighbor
items.informant_bias_notes: Age and birthplace require active reporting by an informant — most likely a household member, possibly a neighbor (same reasoning as a_002).

items.value: Listed in household of Thomas Flynn (head), position and age consistent with son
items.informant: Inferred from household structure — no explicit informant for relationships in 1860 census
items.informant_bias_notes: 1860 census does not state relationships; like the 1850 census, this assertion is inferred from household position, age, and shared surname. The relationship column was not introduced until the 1880 census.

items.informant: James Brown (son-in-law)
items.informant_bias_notes: Son-in-law reporting birth facts decades after the event. Note: death cert says Pennsylvania, but census records say Ireland. Son-in-law may not have known Patrick was born in Ireland.

items.informant: James Brown (son-in-law)
items.informant_bias_notes: Secondary information — son-in-law reporting what he was told about father-in-law's parentage

items.description: Patrick Flynn's birthplace: Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses) vs. Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate)
items.independence_analysis: The two census records (1850, 1860) are independent original sources with different enumerators. The death certificate is a third independent original source. However, the census informants are likely the same household member (Thomas Flynn or wife), so the two census assertions may share a single informant — potentially not fully independent for this fact.
items.weighing_analysis: The census records are contemporary recordings made near the time of Patrick's birth, while the death certificate was created 63 years later. The census informant was likely a household member with firsthand knowledge (primary or indeterminate), while the death certificate informant (son-in-law) is clearly secondary for birth facts. Two contemporary sources outweigh one later recollection by a secondary informant.
items.resolution_rationale: Ireland is accepted as the birthplace. The 1908 death certificate birthplace of 'Pennsylvania' is rejected as a likely error by the son-in-law informant, who may have confused Patrick's place of residence with his place of birth, or may not have known Patrick was born in Ireland before immigrating as a young child.

agent_returns.text:
**Assessment of ps_001 (parentage of Patrick Flynn, q_001): the Probable tier is defensible, but the narrative falls short on GPS components 2, 3, 4 and 5. I wrote nothing.**

**Tier.** Probable is justified.
- Three sources agree that Thomas Flynn is the father. These are the 1850 census (a_004), the 1860 census (a_010) and the 1908 death certificate (a_013, informant son-in-law James Brown).
- The two census relationships are inferred from household position and surname, because those censuses did not state relationships. The death certificate states the father's name, but its informant is secondary.
- Proved is not reached because the evidence is indirect or secondary, and the search is not declared exhaustive.
- Possible would undersell it, since three independent originals converge.

**Component 1, exhaustive search: partial, and ps_001 says so.** It lists the 1850 census, the 1860 census and the death certificate as searched. It names the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses as not yet searched, and the probate search as in progress. The 1880 census is the first to state relationships, so it would corroborate rather than narrow the answer. Probable tolerates that gap, so the tier is not affected. Mother is not addressed, and the tree gives Thomas only.

**Component 2, citations: fails.** The narrative cites by bare id (a_004, a_010, a_013, src_001, src_003, src_004, c_001, plan_001) and has no inline citation. A reader without research.json cannot follow it. The stored citations should be copied in, for example "1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810".

**Component 3, analysis and correlation: weak.**
- The narrative does not state the three-layer classification: original sources, information indeterminate or secondary, and indirect evidence.
- It does not name the informants.
- Its only reasoning is "consistent with" and "none contradicts".
- Its remark that "the supporting assertions are not all direct" is accurate, but it does not say which ones, or that none is direct and primary.

**Component 4, conflicts: weak.**
- c_001 (birthplace) is cited as resolved, which is valid. The conflict is resolved, does not block the question, and has no bearing on identity.
- The narrative does not say what it is about. The conflict is Ireland in the censuses against Pennsylvania on the death certificate.
- It says only "the earlier of the two record groups, on the usual preponderance grounds. See the conflict entry".
- The birthplace dispute does bear on whether the death certificate and the censuses describe the same man. The narrative should say why they are accepted as one person.
- The narrative also does not state that the tree and the question text say Pennsylvania while the conclusion accepts Ireland.
- c_001 lists a_002 as the preferred assertion, but a_002 is not among the assertions returned for q_001.

**Component 5, written conclusion: weak.** The narrative is self-contained in form only. Its hedged wording matches the Probable tier, but it never states what question was answered. It also does not say that the evidence points to the father only, nor that the mother is unidentified.

**Other defects:**
- The summary tells the reader to see "plan_001" for what would advance the tier, instead of naming the records.
- The narrative says the evidence rests on a_004, a_010 and a_013, but pe_005 notes that the death certificate lists James Brown as informant. That detail is absent from the narrative.

**Tree.** I1 is linked to Thomas Flynn (I2) as parent, and I2 has three children (I1, I3, I4). The concluded ParentChild link is encoded. I did not check the tree's source references.

**Question status.** q_001 is still `in_progress`, although a summary exists. The project context flags "concluded while blocked: re-conclude ps_001".

**Gaps for the next round (not defects of ps_001).** These sources exist in research.json, have zero linked assertions and were never extracted:
- **src_006:** will of Thomas Flynn, 1881. It could name Patrick as a son and heir, which is direct, primary evidence.
- **src_008:** 1881 deed from Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn. It may state a relationship.
- **src_005:** 1845 St. Mary's baptism of Patrick Flynn. It could name the parents, including the mother. It also tests the Ireland versus Pennsylvania conflict.
- **src_009:** 1908 obituary. It may name family members.
- **src_007:** 1905 birth certificate of Mary Elizabeth Flynn. It is probably not relevant to this parentage question.

The will, the baptism and possibly the deed are direct and original. Extracting them could raise the tier to Proved if they agree and the search is declared exhaustive. The baptism could also change the answer: it would identify the mother, and it would affect the birthplace conflict.

These five sources also carry only rough working citations (some missing volume and page, or naming the wrong creator), so each needs a complete citation before it is cited.

**Recommended next steps:**
- Rewrite ps_001's narrative and exhaustive-search summary to fix components 2 to 5. Use stored citations, informants, classifications and the full conflict reasoning.
- Route record-extraction to the unextracted sources above.
- Route research-plan for the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and the probate search.

---

This looks likely but not certain: the records point to Thomas Flynn as Patrick Flynn's father. Three records agree on this. Two are census listings that place Patrick, aged about 5 and 15, in Thomas's household. The third is Patrick's 1908 death certificate, which names Thomas as father, though the person giving that information was his son-in-law. No record yet states the relationship firsthand, and the mother is not identified. Not yet searched are the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses and the probate search. Also not yet read are a 1881 will, a 1881 deed, an 1845 baptism record and a 1908 obituary.

Next, the write-up of this finding should be tightened, and the will, deed, baptism and obituary should be read for firsthand evidence of the relationship.

Here is the proof-conclusion agent's report:

---

**Result:** `ps_001` appended at **Possible** (shortfall: `gap`). `q_001` is left open; nothing was written to the tree yet.

---

### Gate Check
All three preconditions passed: assertions carry reasoned classifications, I1 has linked identity assertions, and no conflicts are registered.

### Tier: Possible
The evidence supports only a *possible* conclusion because:
- Elijah Wilkins (I1) died **after the 1870 census** and **before the 1885 estate administration** in Muhlenberg County, Kentucky.
- A **namesake** (Elijah Wilkins, born ~1822, `ns_001`) in the same county is not yet excluded.
- The administrator link to I1 is only inferred, and the source is a derivative index.

### Why the Tree Was Not Updated
`tree_edit` refused to attach the bounded Death fact while the namesake remains unresolved and the estate record is not firmly tied to I1. Jesse Wilkins (I2) also lacks a linked identity assertion.

---

### Narrative Summary
> Elijah Wilkins, born about 1814 in Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, **probably died between 1870 and 1885** in that county — a *possible* conclusion, not a firm one. The 1885 county court records show his estate was administered by Jesse Wilkins; the 1870 census shows him still alive. A second Elijah Wilkins (born ~1822) lived in the same county, and nothing yet excludes him as the decedent. Kentucky kept no statewide death certificates before 1911.

---

### Next Steps
1. **Person-evidence:** Tie the estate record and Jesse as administrator to I1 against the namesake.
2. **Re-run proof-conclusion** to write the Death fact and resolve q_001.
3. **What would raise the tier:** The **1880 Muhlenberg County census** would narrow the bracket; the **original order book and estate file** (listing heirs) would secure identity. Use `research-plan` to schedule both.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
When and where did Elijah Wilkins (born about 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky) die?

## Answer (possible)
Elijah Wilkins may have died after the 1870 census and before the 1885 term of the Muhlenberg County Court, in Muhlenberg County, Kentucky. This is a bounded, tentative answer; an exact date is not established by the evidence gathered so far, and identity of the decedent with I1 is not yet secure.

## Evidence
- **Upper bound.** The Muhlenberg County Court order book records the administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, with Jesse Wilkins as administrator, 1885 term (Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, Court Order Books, administration of the estate of Elijah Wilkins, deceased, intestate, Jesse Wilkins administrator, 1885 term; digital images, FamilySearch.org). The source is a derivative full-text index of the order-book page; the original order book was not separately imaged. The clerk is the informant; his proximity to the death is unknown, information quality is indeterminate, and the death timing is inferred (the entry says he was dead, not when he died).
- **Lower bound.** Existing tree fact F2 (Residence, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky, 1870) shows I1 alive at that census. F2 carries no linked source entry in research.json.
- **Documented negative.** No Kentucky death certificate exists for him: statewide registration began in 1911, and a search of Kentucky death collections returned nothing (12 results examined).
- **Place.** The estate was administered in Muhlenberg County, which is where he lived in 1870; the record does not state a place of death.

## Identity problem
A second Elijah Wilkins, born about 1822, is recorded in Muhlenberg County (namesake ns_001). Nothing in the order entry itself distinguishes the two men. ---

**Proof Summary Written — `ps_001` (Question q_001 resolved)**

**Tier: Probable** *(paternity probable; maternity not proved)*

---

### Proof Narrative

Patrick Flynn, born about 1845 and died in 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, was most likely the son of Thomas Flynn. Patrick appears as a child in Thomas Flynn's household in the 1850 and 1860 censuses. His 1908 death certificate also names Thomas as his father. The censuses don't state relationships, and the death certificate's information came from Patrick's son-in-law, so this is a likely finding and not a certain one. Patrick's mother has not been identified. The only candidate, a widow named Bridget Flynn in the 1870 census, has nothing but a shared common surname to connect her to the family. A thorough search is not yet complete. Thomas's marriage and probate records, the 1880 census, Patrick's marriage record, and his obituary have not been searched.

---

### Key Findings

- **Paternity (Probable):** The 1850 and 1860 censuses place Patrick in Thomas Flynn's household; the 1908 death certificate names Thomas directly (but via a secondary informant — Patrick's son-in-law).
- **Maternity (Not Proved):** Bridget Flynn (I3) is only a speculative link with a vanishingly low match score and no corroborating evidence.
- **Tree updated:** A ParentChild relationship was written — Thomas Flynn (I2) → Patrick Flynn (I1) — citing the census (S1) and death certificate (S3). No mother relationship was added.
- **Conflict c_001** (birthplace conflict) is resolved and cited in the summary.
- **Research is not exhaustive.** Still unsearched: Thomas's probate, marriage, or death record; the 1880 census; Patrick's marriage record to Mary Doyle; and his obituary.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Run proof-conclusion for q_002**, which is marked resolved but has no proof summary.
2. **Plan a research search** for the unsearched records above — especially Thomas's probate and marriage record and Patrick's obituary — to strengthen the paternity finding and open a path to identifying the mother.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)

**Conclusion.** The evidence points to Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland) as the father of Patrick Flynn, at the **probable** tier. Patrick's mother is **not proved**: no record in hand names her.

### Paternity
Patrick Flynn, age 5, is enumerated in the household of Thomas Flynn, head, in the 1850 census ("1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026."). The Ancestry index of the same census (a derivative) transcribes the household consistently and adds no independent information. In 1860 Patrick, age 15, is again in a Thomas Flynn household in the same county ("1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026."). Both are original sources, but neither census states relationships; the parent-child link is inferred from household position, age and shared surname, so the information is indirect and its informant unknown. The two enumerations share a head and likely a household informant, so they corroborate continuity of residence more than they are independent witnesses to parentage.

The direct statement comes from the death certificate ("Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026."), which names Thomas Flynn as father. The informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown, who was not present at the birth: the information is secondary and was given 60 years or more after Patrick's childhood. It is nonetheless an independent line from the censuses, since its informant is unconnected to the enumerations, and it agrees with them.

### Conflict accounted for
The censuses give Ireland as Patrick's birthplace; the death certificate gives Pennsylvania (resolved conflict c_001, resolved in favor of Ireland: two contemporary records against a secondary informant's later recollection). The dispute is about the birthplace, not the father's name, and the certificate's error does not touch its statement of Thomas as father; the same son-in-law's limited knowledge does, however, lower the weight of that statement, which is part of why the tier is not higher. Existing tree fact F3 (Birth, ~1818, Ireland) for Thomas is consistent with a family that came from Ireland; it carries no linked source entry in research.json.

### Maternity
Bridget Flynn, a widow aged 52 in the 1870 census, is the only candidate considered ("1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026."). The record names no husband and no child, Thomas Flynn is absent from it, and Flynn is a common surname in the county; the identity link is rated speculative (match score 0.0002). The two Pottsville baptisms (1870, 1872) are for children of Patrick Flynn and Mary Doyle; they bear on Patrick's own family, name no grandparents, and say nothing about his mother. Nothing here supports Bridget as mother, and the question of Patrick's mother remains unresolved pending a marriage or probate record for Thomas Flynn, Patrick's own marriage record, the 1880 census or an obituary.

### Tier
Paternity is probable: direct but secondary-informant evidence agrees with two original but indirect census placements, and the one conflict is resolved. It is not proved because the research is not declared exhaustive, the census evidence is inferential, and no probate, marriage or other record independent of those informants has been searched. Maternity is not proved. Conclusions are open to revision if new evidence emerges.

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. entry.narrative_markdown:
## Question
Did Person A (born 1856, Germany) leave an accessible South Dakota death certificate, and when did he die?

## Answer (possible)
Person A most likely died about 1935 at or near Gregory, Gregory County, South Dakota. No death certificate has been found in the sources reached so far. This remains a possible answer: the year rests on one derivative source plus one original record that does not state a death date, and no record giving an exact date has been seen.

## Evidence
- Find a Grave Index: "Find a Grave Index," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVLD-NSQ7 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, memorial #88075502. It gives death 1935 and burial at Gregory. It is derivative; the contributor is unidentified, so informant knowledge is unknown and the information quality is indeterminate.
- Grave registration: "South Dakota, Grave Registration Records, 1939-1942," database with images, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:CYCQ-NRW2 : accessed 6 August 2026), entry for Person A, Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota. It is an original record created 1939-1942, but the death date is blank. It records burial at Gregory IOOF Cemetery and age at death 79 (informant unknown). Age is indirect evidence: with birth year 1856, age 79 is consistent with death in 1935 (and, without a known birthday, does not by itself exclude 1936). The record was made after the death, so it is not primary information about the date.
- Existing tree facts: F1 (Birth, Germany, 1856) and F2 (Residence, Gregory, Gregory, South Dakota, 1935) were already in the tree; F1 supplies the birth year used for the age calculation and F2 places him at Gregory in 1935. Neither carries a linked source entry in research.json.
- Negative search: FamilySearch-indexed SD death records, searched under two surname spellings, returned no death certificate for Person A (log_003, log_004). FamilySearch's index does not cover every certificate, so this shows the certificate is not accessible there, not that none exists.

## Correlation and conflicts
The two sources agree on place and are consistent on year; no conflicts are registered. They are not independent in any strong sense, because neither states the date from first-hand knowledge. Hence the possible tier.

## What could resolve it
A request to the South Dakota State Archives / state vital records for a 1935 (or 1936) certificate, browsing unindexed FamilySearch death microfilm, Gregory-area newspaper obituaries, and cemetery or county burial and probate records.

## Tier
Possible, shortfall gap. The conclusion is a bounded death (about 1935, Gregory SD); the existence of a certificate remains open pending the unsearched archives.

A marriage record or a Flynn relative appearing alongside Patrick in a later census could still settle the question. If you'd like to continue, use the research-plan agent to map out those next steps.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Who was the father of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, d. 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion (not proved).** The evidence gathered so far does not identify Patrick's father. Two men, Thomas Flynn and Michael Flynn, are equally plausible candidates, and nothing found separates them. No tree relationship is asserted.

### The subject is firmly identified, his parentage is not
The 1908 death certificate (Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 5 May 2026) is an original record, with primary information on the death from the attending physician, and places the death on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County. It is the one record likely to name a father, and the father field is blank: the informant, son-in-law James Brown, reported the name as unknown. This is negative evidence of a weak kind. It shows the family's memory of the father had faded by 1908. It does not point to any candidate.

### Two equally fitting childhood households in 1850
The 1850 census (NARA M432, roll 810) lists two Irish-born boys named Patrick Flynn of fitting age in Schuylkill County:
- Age 5 (about 1845) in the household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, family 91 (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026).
- Age 6 (about 1844) in the household of Michael Flynn, dwelling 210, family 233, in a different enumeration district (1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 210, family 233, Michael Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026).

Both records are originals, but the 1850 census does not state relationships, and the informant is unknown. Each child's tie to the head is only inferred from household position, and the information quality is indeterminate. The ages are 5 and 6 against a subject born about 1845, and a one-year difference is well within ordinary census age error, so age does not choose between them. Each household therefore supports only a conditional claim: if this boy is our Patrick, then this head is a candidate father. These are hypotheses h_001 (Thomas) and h_002 (Michael); neither is contradicted and neither can be eliminated.

### The 1860 census breaks the chain
In 1860 a Patrick Flynn, age 15, appears as a boarder and coal laborer in the Owen Donnelly household, dwelling 305 (1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 305, Owen Donnelly household, Patrick Flynn (boarder); NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026). This is an original record with primary information on his residence, and it fits the subject. No Flynn adult lives with him, and neither Thomas nor Michael is a near neighbor. The record therefore does not link him back to either 1850 household. It also shows he was living apart from any parent by age 15, which fits a father who had died or moved away, but that fits both candidates equally.

### Parish registers
A search of the FamilySearch and NLI Catholic parish registers for a Patrick Flynn baptism in Schuylkill County and the Tipperary emigrant cohort, 1843-1850, found no baptism naming a father. The record that would answer the question directly was not located. Its absence is not evidence for either candidate.

### Why no candidate is preferred
There are two candidates, no direct evidence, and no record that connects the adult Patrick to either household. The only evidence is indirect, rests on an unverified assumption of identity for each child, and is symmetrical between the two men. Preferring one would be a guess. No conflict between sources is registered, because the records do not contradict one another. They simply fail to discriminate.

### What would settle it
The present evidence does not establish the father. The answer remains open pending record types not yet searched: Patrick's marriage record, which often names parents; the 1870 and 1880 censuses, which could show him near a Flynn relative or one candidate household; an obituary or burial record; naturalization papers; and any family Bible or church record. A marriage record or a kinsman in a later census could resolve the question and not merely corroborate it, so these searches should be planned before the finding is treated as final.

### Tier
**Not proved.** The identity of the subject is secure, but the evidence is indirect and divides evenly between two candidates. Any proof is open to revision if new evidence surfaces.
